evidence.query: Bank change announcement on supplier website
evidence.finding: The supplier's website announced on 1 August 2026 a move to SEB with bankgiro 5678-9019.
The announcement says invoices to the old bankgiro are still paid as normal until 30 September.

evidence.query: Compare new invoice to last 5 invoices
evidence.finding: Contact email faktura@sveakontor.se matches the address on all five prior invoices.
Invoice amount 15,100 SEK and 30 day terms are in line with prior invoices from this supplier.
All five prior invoices used the old bankgiro 234-5676; this is the first invoice with the new account.
The new bankgiro has a valid check digit and is registered to the supplier at Bankgirot.
The old bankgiro is also validly registered to the supplier at Bankgirot.

points: The new bankgiro was opened only 24 days ago, and the payment history to it is zero after 12 payments to the old account.
The website announcement is easy to fake or spoof; a matching website notice is exactly what an attacker who compromised the site or email would arrange.
The announcement itself says the old bankgiro is still paid as normal until 30 September, so there is no business reason to switch now on this invoice.
The matching contact email faktura@sveakontor.se proves nothing if the supplier's mail or website has been taken over; the same channel would carry the fake instruction.
A bank change after 12 clean payments is the textbook pattern for supplier invoice fraud and deserves a call-back on a known phone number before any payment.
arguments.strongest_point: The supplier's own announcement says the old account is still paid as normal until 30 September, so paying the brand new 24 day old account today gives up a safe option for no reason.

points: The new bankgiro 5678-9019 is registered to the supplier itself at Bankgirot, not to a third party.
The supplier announced the move to SEB with bankgiro 5678-9019 on their own website on 1 August 2026.
The invoice contact email faktura@sveakontor.se matches the email on all five prior invoices from this supplier.
The invoice amount of 15,100 SEK and 30 day terms match the pattern of prior invoices.
The supplier has been active at the same Stockholm address in the company register since 2009.
arguments.strongest_point: Two independent sources confirm the new account belongs to the supplier: Bankgirot has it registered to the supplier, and the supplier's own website announced the switch to this exact bankgiro on 1 August 2026.

points: Ownership records at Bankgirot only show the name on the account, not whether the account was opened by the real supplier or by someone impersonating them 24 days ago.
A website announcement and a Bankgirot registration can both be arranged by the same attacker in the same week, so they are not truly independent.
The supplier's own announcement says the old account is still paid as normal until 30 September, so the safe path is to pay the old account we have used 12 times.
Matching email, amount and terms are exactly what a fraudster copies from a prior invoice; they do not confirm the new account.
Standard practice on any bank change after 12 clean payments is a call-back to the phone number we already have on file before releasing 15,100 SEK.
arguments.strongest_point: The supplier's own announcement says the old bankgiro is paid as normal until 30 September, so pay the account we have used 12 times and confirm the new one by a call-back on the phone number we already have on file.

points: The opponent's strongest point actually helps us: the transition window until 30 September is public and matches the supplier's announcement, which is exactly the kind of detail a fraudster staging an urgent switch would not include.
Two independent sources confirm ownership of the new account: Bankgirot has 5678-9019 registered to the supplier, and this is a bank-controlled record, not the supplier's website.
The account belongs to the supplier itself, not a private person or third party, so even in the worst case funds land in the supplier's own account.
A quick call-back to the phone number we have on file for prior invoices resolves any residual doubt without blocking a legitimate supplier we have paid 12 times.
Blocking a 15,100 SEK invoice that matches prior amount, terms, email and supplier identity risks a real relationship for a scenario with no third-party account and no risk flags at the bank.
arguments.strongest_point: Bankgirot independently confirms the new bankgiro 5678-9019 is registered to the supplier, so this is not a payment being diverted to an outsider; a call-back on the phone number we already have on file is the proportionate check, not a block.

verdict.reasoning: The evidence for the new account is strong: Bankgirot has it registered to the supplier, and the supplier's website announced the switch. But the new account is only 24 days old and this is the first invoice on it, so a quick confirmation is proportionate. The supplier's own announcement also says the old account is still valid until 30 September, giving a safe fallback.
verdict.recommended_action: Before paying, confirm the new bankgiro 5678-9019 by contacting the supplier on the email we have on file, faktura@sveakontor.se; if any doubt remains, pay the old bankgiro 234-5676 which is still valid until 30 September.
